Spending time at the Hotel Messina is a pleasure, a lazy holiday on which not a lot happens, very charmingly.

This is Shakespeare in the swing age, its drama turned into stylish screwball comedy.
It’s a glittery, apolitical production but it’s well cast, stylish, summery stuff.
Katherine Parkinson has star quality, but sarcasm is now such a part of her stage persona that she struggles to hit the occasionally more serious notes required of Beatrice.
All part of the fun in church hall am-dram, perhaps — but not at the National Theatre.
For anyone who wants to see Parkinson, Heffernan or Godwin giving their best work, it’s sorely disappointing.

This is light entertainment for a summer evening that takes us to Mediterranean sunshine while keeping us cool indoors.
It’s all very larky and witty, with giggle-worthy sight gags involving a trolley, a hammock and a beach hut in the twin scenes that entrap Beatrice and Benedict into coupledom.
If the emotional layers of Much Ado are a little fudged, there is still plenty to admire in the spectacular clothes by Evie Gurney.
However, Simon Godwin's new staging, transported from 16th century Sicily to an early 20th century Mediterranean Hotel, fails to fully ignite.
Godwin – an old hand at Shakespeare having done Romeo & Juliet, Twelfth Night and Antony & Cleopatra for the National – keeps the tone from veering into try-hard territory.
That’s the pleasure of a production like this: “leger” as the French group said, and gleefully farcical at times.

This is a thoroughly enjoyable production and I was very impressed by the enthusiasm it generated among the wide spectrum of audience, young and not-so-young that was present on the night that I attended.
Simon Godwin’s Much Ado about Nothing blazes with sultry Latin flare.
Godwin’s constables – all in mint-green hotel flummery – strike off each clear twittery by turns so we savour it.
Godwin’s feelgood show is stylish, escapist entertainment with high production values that doesn’t quite hit the romantic or comedic sweet spots.

cn.t: Godwin's 1930s Riviera staging dazzles visually but divides critics—the Art Deco design earns near-universal praise, while Parkinson and Heffernan's chemistry sparks debate, leaving some charmed and others cold.
